title: Math of Space: Surface Area and Volume

topics.title: Surface versus space: cuboids in layers

learn.hook: A 1 × 1 × 8 stick of clay and a 2 × 2 × 2 cube use the same clay. Which needs more wrapping paper?
points: Every solid has a surface (measured as area, in square units) and takes up space (volume, in cubic units).
Volume as layers: stack thin layers each with the base area; volume = base area × height. For a cuboid that is l × w × h.
The same volume can have different surface areas: 1 × 1 × 8 and 2 × 2 × 2 both have volume 8, but surface areas 34 and 24. Compact shapes lose less heat and need less packaging.
If the three face areas of a cuboid are A₁ = lw, A₂ = wh, A₃ = hl, then A₁ × A₂ × A₃ = (lwh)², so V = √(A₁A₂A₃).

example.q: A cuboid's faces have areas 12 cm², 15 cm² and 20 cm². Find its volume.

learn.reallife: Laddoo boxes and milk cartons are shaped to hold a lot with as little cardboard as possible.

topics.title: Surface area of cuboids, cubes and cylinders

learn.hook: How much paper do you need to gift-wrap a box of sweets for Diwali? That is a surface area question!
points: Surface area is the total area of all the outer faces of a solid, measured in square units.
Cuboid (l × b × h): total surface area = 2(lb + bh + hl). The four walls of a room (lateral surface) = 2(l + b) × h.
Cube of edge a: total surface area = 6a²; lateral surface area = 4a².
Cylinder of radius r and height h: curved surface area = 2πrh; total surface area = 2πr(r + h).
Open shapes (a box without a lid, a pipe without ends) need only the faces that are really there.

example.q: A closed cylindrical tin has radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. How much metal sheet is needed to make it? (Use π = 22/7.)

learn.reallife: Painters charge by the square metre of wall, and tin factories order metal sheets by the surface area of the cans they make.

quiz.q: Find the total surface area of a cube of edge 5 cm.
quiz.explain: A cube has 6 square faces, each 5 × 5 = 25 cm². Total = 6 × 25 = 150 cm².
quiz.mistake: Finds the volume (125) instead of the surface area

quiz.q: Find the total surface area of a cuboid 10 cm × 6 cm × 4 cm.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double (124) or finds the volume (240)

quiz.q: Find the curved surface area of a cylinder with radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.mistake: Includes the two circular ends (748) or finds the volume (1540)

quiz.q: Arjun paints the four walls of a room 5 m long, 4 m wide and 3 m high at ₹20 per m². What does it cost?
quiz.explain: Area of four walls = 2(5 + 4) × 3 = 54 m². Cost = 54 × 20 = ₹1080.
quiz.mistake: Uses the volume (60 m³) instead of the wall area, getting ₹1200

quiz.q: If the edge of a cube is doubled, what happens to its surface area?
quiz.explain: Surface area is 6a². With edge 2a it becomes 6(2a)² = 24a², which is 4 times 6a².
steps: Answer: It becomes 4 times as big
quiz.mistake: Thinks doubling the edge doubles every measurement, or uses the volume rule (8 times)

quiz.q: A road roller is a cylinder of radius 0.7 m and length 2 m. How much ground does it level in 10 full turns? (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.explain: In one turn it covers its curved surface: 2 × 22/7 × 0.7 × 2 = 8.8 m². In 10 turns: 88 m².
quiz.mistake: Gives the area for just one turn

quiz.q: An open box (no lid) measures 10 cm × 8 cm × 5 cm. What is the area of cardboard needed?
quiz.explain: Four walls: 2(10 + 8) × 5 = 180 cm². Add the base 10 × 8 = 80 cm². Total = 260 cm².
quiz.mistake: Includes the lid (340) or forgets the base (180)

quiz.q: Find the total surface area of a closed cylindrical drum of radius 14 cm and height 6 cm. (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.mistake: Finds only the curved surface (528) and forgets the two ends

teach.ask: Gappu wants to cover a gift box with paper: "How do I know how much paper I need?"
teach.praise: Find the area of every face and add them all up. For a box that is 2(lb + bh + hl). Wrapping done!
teach.nudge: How many faces does the box have? What do you do with the area of each one?

revise.summary: Surface area is the total outer area. Cuboid 2(lb + bh + hl), cube 6a², cylinder curved 2πrh and total 2πr(r + h). Open shapes need only the faces present.
focus: Find surface areas of cuboids, cubes and cylinders.
remember: Cylinder r = 7, h = 10: CSA 440 cm², TSA 748 cm².
Doubling a cube's edge makes its area 4 times.
traps: Don't give volume instead of area.
Leave out faces that are not there (lid, ends).
Area scales by 4, not 2 or 8, when the edge doubles.

topics.title: Packing, painted cubes and integer boxes

learn.hook: Dip a 4 × 4 × 4 cube of small cubes in paint. How many small cubes have no paint at all? Only the hidden heart!
points: Packing: the number of small boxes a × b × c that fit (in the same orientation) in a box L × W × H is (L ÷ a) × (W ÷ b) × (H ÷ c), using whole numbers only.
Painted n × n × n cube cut into unit cubes: 3 faces painted: 8 (corners); 2 faces: 12(n − 2) (edges); 1 face: 6(n − 2)² (face centres); 0 faces: (n − 2)³ (inside).
Cuboids with whole-number edges and surface area S: solve lw + wh + hl = S/2. For S = 22 there are exactly two: 1 × 1 × 5 and 1 × 2 × 3.

example.q: A 5 × 5 × 5 painted cube is cut into unit cubes. Count the cubes with 2 faces painted and with none.

learn.reallife: Warehouse managers plan how many cartons fit on a truck using this packing calculation.

topics.title: Cylinders: discs, ratios and percentage changes

learn.hook: Stack khakhras one on top of another and you've built a cylinder!
points: A right circular cylinder has two equal circular bases, every cross-section parallel to the base is the same circle, and its axis is perpendicular to the base.
Think of a cylinder as a stack of thin discs (like khakhras or coins): each has area πr², and the stack has height h, so V = πr²h.
Ratios: if the radius is multiplied by k, volume is multiplied by k² (height fixed); if the height is multiplied by k, volume is multiplied by k.
Percentage change: radius up 10% (× 1.1) makes volume × 1.21, a 21% increase. Curved surface area 2πrh grows by the same factor as r × h.

example.q: Cylinder A has radius 3 cm and height 8 cm; cylinder B has radius 6 cm and height 4 cm. Compare their volumes.
example.answer: B has twice the volume of A

learn.reallife: A stack of ₹10 coins is a cylinder; doubling the stack doubles the volume, but a coin twice as wide holds four times the metal.

A cylinder's cross-sections parallel to its base are all equal circles.

A stack of coins approximates a cylinder.
Thin discs stacked up.

One circular base and an apex
A curved surface with no flat faces

Its axis is perpendicular to the bases.
Answer: Two equal circular bases with the axis perpendicular to them

quiz.q: Why is V = πr²h for a cylinder?
options: It is a stack of discs of area πr² piled to height h
Because it is a cone tripled
quiz.explain: Base area × height, like any prism.
steps: A cylinder is a stack of thin discs.
Each disc has area πr²; the stack is h high.
Answer: It is a stack of discs of area πr² piled to height h
quiz.mistake: Uses the circumference instead of the area

quiz.q: A cylindrical glass has radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. Another has radius 6 cm and height 2.5 cm. Which holds more?

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "If I double a cylinder's radius, does its volume double?"
teach.praise: Correct! Volume depends on r², so doubling r makes it 4 times!
teach.nudge: How does the radius appear in πr²h? What happens to r² if r doubles?

revise.summary: A cylinder is a stack of discs, so V = πr²h. Volume scales with r² and with h, so a 10% larger radius gives 21% more volume.
remember: r = 3, h = 8 vs r = 6, h = 4: volumes 72π and 144π.
traps: Volume depends on r², not r.
Don't double a percentage change.
A wider glass does not always hold more.

topics.title: Volume of cylinders, cones and spheres

learn.hook: Fill a cone with water three times and pour it into a cylinder of the same base and height: it fills up exactly. Maths predicted it!
points: Volume is the space a solid takes up, measured in cubic units. 1000 cm³ = 1 litre, and 1 m³ = 1000 litres.
Cuboid: V = l × b × h. Cube: V = a³.
Cylinder: V = πr²h (base area × height).
Cone: V = ⅓πr²h, exactly one third of a cylinder with the same base and height.
Sphere: V = (4/3)πr³. Hemisphere: V = (2/3)πr³. When a solid is melted and recast, its volume stays the same.

example.q: A cone-shaped heap of wheat has radius 7 m and height 3 m. Find its volume. (Use π = 22/7.)

learn.reallife: Water tankers, LPG cylinders, ice-cream cones and gol gappas all have volumes that companies calculate with these formulas.

quiz.mistake: Finds the curved surface area (440) instead of the volume

quiz.q: Find the volume of a cone with radius 7 cm and height 12 cm. (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ⅓ and gives the cylinder's volume (1848)

quiz.q: Find the volume of a sphere of radius 21 cm. (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.mistake: Uses the hemisphere formula (19404) or forgets the 4/3 (29106)

quiz.q: A cone and a cylinder have the same radius and the same height. How many cones of water fill the cylinder?
quiz.explain: The cone's volume is ⅓πr²h, one third of the cylinder's πr²h, so 3 cones fill it.
steps: So the cylinder holds 3 cones of water.
quiz.mistake: Writes the fraction 1/3 instead of the number of cones

quiz.q: A water tank is a cuboid 2 m long, 1.5 m wide and 1 m deep. How many litres does it hold when full?
quiz.explain: Volume = 2 × 1.5 × 1 = 3 m³, and 1 m³ = 1000 litres, so the tank holds 3000 litres.
quiz.mistake: Uses 100 litres per cubic metre instead of 1000

quiz.q: Find the volume of a hemispherical bowl of radius 21 cm. (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.explain: V = (2/3)πr³ = 2/3 × 22/7 × 9261 = 19404 cm³, half of the whole sphere.
quiz.mistake: Uses the whole sphere's volume (38808) instead of half

quiz.q: A metal sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and recast into small spheres of radius 2 cm. How many small spheres are made?
quiz.explain: Volume grows with r³. (6 ÷ 2)³ = 3³ = 27, so the big sphere has 27 times the volume of a small one.
quiz.mistake: Divides the radii (3) or compares areas (9) instead of volumes

quiz.q: A cube has total surface area 150 cm². What is its volume?
quiz.explain: 6a² = 150 gives a² = 25 and a = 5 cm. Volume = 5³ = 125 cm³.
quiz.mistake: Uses a² = 25 as the volume, or squares 25 to get 625

teach.ask: Gappu has a cone and a cylinder of the same size base and height: "Which holds more water, and how much more?"
teach.praise: The cylinder holds πr²h, and the cone only ⅓ of that. So it takes three cones to fill the cylinder. Splash!
teach.nudge: How many cones of water do you need to fill the cylinder? What fraction is that?

revise.summary: Volume is the space a solid fills. Cylinder πr²h, cone ⅓πr²h, sphere (4/3)πr³, hemisphere (2/3)πr³. 1000 cm³ = 1 litre and recasting keeps volume the same.
focus: Find volumes of cylinders, cones and spheres.
Convert cm³ and m³ to litres.
remember: Cone = ⅓ of the cylinder with the same base and height.
traps: Don't forget the ⅓ for a cone.
A hemisphere is half a sphere.
1 m³ is 1000 litres, not 100.

topics.title: Cones: how they form and where we meet them

learn.hook: Spin a set square around one of its short edges really fast: the blur you see is a cone!
points: A right circular cone is formed by rotating a right triangle about one of its legs: that leg becomes the height h, the other leg the radius r, and the hypotenuse the slant height l.
Rotating the same triangle about the other leg gives a different cone (radius and height swap).
Problems: a birthday cap needs paper = curved surface πrl; a conical tent needs canvas πrl and holds air ⅓πr²h; a tarpaulin to cover a heap uses πrl.
A conical cup filled to half its depth holds only 1/8 of its full volume, because the water forms a smaller cone with half the radius and half the height: (½)² × ½ = 1/8.

example.q: A right triangle has legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Find the volume of the cone made by rotating it about the 8 cm leg. (π = 3.14)

learn.reallife: Ice-cream cones, traffic cones, mehndi cones and tent tops are all cones.

quiz.q: A right triangle with legs 3 cm and 4 cm is rotated about the 4 cm leg. What is the radius of the cone?
quiz.explain: The leg it spins around is the height; the other leg sweeps out the radius.
steps: The leg it spins around becomes the height (4 cm).
The other leg sweeps out the radius: 3 cm.

quiz.q: For the same rotation, what is the slant height?
quiz.explain: The hypotenuse √(9 + 16) = 5 becomes the slant height.
steps: The hypotenuse becomes the slant height.
quiz.mistake: Adds the legs

quiz.mistake: Uses the height instead of the slant height

quiz.q: How much air is inside that tent? (π = 22/7)
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ⅓

quiz.q: A conical paper cup holds 240 ml when full. How much does it hold when filled to half its depth?
quiz.explain: The water cone has half the radius and half the height: 1/8 of 240.
steps: At half depth, the water cone has half the radius and half the height.
quiz.mistake: Thinks half the depth means half the volume

quiz.q: Rotating a right triangle about its hypotenuse gives:
options: two cones joined at their bases
quiz.explain: Each part of the triangle on either side of the altitude sweeps a cone.
steps: The altitude to the hypotenuse splits the triangle into two right triangles.
Each sweeps a cone about the hypotenuse.
The cones share a circular base.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How can a triangle turn into a cone?"
teach.praise: Brilliant! Spin a right triangle about a leg: that leg is the height and the other is the radius!
teach.nudge: What do you do with the triangle? Which side becomes the height?

revise.summary: Rotating a right triangle about a leg gives a cone: that leg is the height, the other the radius, the hypotenuse the slant height. Caps and tents use πrl; air inside uses ⅓πr²h.
focus: Find the cone made by rotating a triangle.
Solve cap, tent and tarpaulin problems.
remember: Rotating about the hypotenuse → two cones.
traps: The axis leg is the height, not the radius.
Use slant height for πrl.
Half the depth is not half the volume.

topics.title: Surface area of cones and spheres

learn.hook: A birthday cap, an ice-cream cone and a cricket ball: two of these are cones and one is a sphere. How much material covers each?
points: A right circular cone has radius r, height h and slant height l, where l = √(r² + h²).
Curved surface area of a cone = πrl; total surface area = πr(l + r).
Surface area of a sphere of radius r = 4πr².
A hemisphere has curved surface area 2πr² and, with its flat circular face, total surface area 3πr².
If the radius of a sphere doubles, its surface area becomes 4 times as big.

example.q: A conical birthday cap has radius 7 cm and height 24 cm. How much paper is needed for it? (Use π = 22/7.)

learn.reallife: Tent-makers measure canvas for conical tents with πrl, and football manufacturers need 4πr² of leather for each ball.

games.title: Curved surface check
items: The slant height of a cone is always longer than its height
l = √(r² + h²), which is more than h whenever r > 0.
A sphere's surface area is 4 times the area of its biggest circle
The biggest circle has area πr², and the sphere's surface is 4πr².
Curved surface area of a cone = πrh
It uses the slant height l, not the height h: πrl.
Doubling the radius of a ball doubles its surface area
Surface area depends on r², so it becomes 4 times as big.
The curved surface of a hemisphere is half the surface of the full sphere
Half of 4πr² is 2πr².

quiz.q: Find the surface area of a sphere of radius 7 cm. (Use π = 22/7.)

quiz.q: Find the total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius 7 cm. (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.explain: TSA = curved part + flat circle = 2πr² + πr² = 3πr² = 3 × 22/7 × 49 = 462 cm².
steps: TSA of a solid hemisphere = 2πr² + πr² = 3πr².
quiz.mistake: Forgets the flat circular face and gives 2πr² = 308

quiz.q: A joker's cap is a cone of radius 7 cm and slant height 12 cm. How much sheet is needed to make it? (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.explain: A cap has no base, so we need only the curved surface: πrl = 22/7 × 7 × 12 = 264 cm².
steps: A cap has no base: only the curved surface.
quiz.mistake: Adds the base circle (418) even though a cap is open at the bottom

quiz.q: A ball has surface area 154 cm². What is its radius? (Use π = 22/7.)

quiz.q: A hemispherical bowl has radius 10.5 cm. What is the area of its inner curved surface? (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.explain: Curved surface of a hemisphere = 2πr² = 2 × 22/7 × 10.5 × 10.5 = 693 cm².
quiz.mistake: Uses 4πr² (the whole sphere, 1386) instead of half of it

quiz.q: Find the total surface area of a solid cone with radius 7 cm and slant height 25 cm. (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.mistake: Gives only the curved surface (550), forgetting the base

teach.ask: Gappu holds an ice-cream cone: "How much wafer is used to make the cone? Do I use its height?"
teach.praise: Use the slant height l, found by Pythagoras from r and h, and the curved surface is πrl. Wafer-thin and exactly right!
teach.nudge: Is the wafer's length along the side the same as the cone's straight-up height? Which one goes into the formula?

revise.summary: A cone has slant height l = √(r² + h²), curved area πrl and total area πr(l + r). A sphere has area 4πr²; a hemisphere has curved area 2πr² and total 3πr².
focus: Find curved and total surface areas.
Choose curved or total area from the context.
remember: Sphere r = 7: 616 cm²; hemisphere TSA 462 cm².
A cap has no base: only πrl.
traps: Don't add r and h for the slant height.
Sphere area is 4πr², not πr².
Include the flat face for a solid hemisphere.

learn.hook: The great pyramids of Egypt and the sharp peak of a temple tower share one formula!
points: A pyramid has a polygon base and triangular faces that meet at a point called the apex. Egyptian pyramids are square pyramids; mountain peaks and some temple roofs look pyramidal.
Volume of any pyramid = ⅓ × base area × height (height measured straight up from base to apex).
Surface area = base area + areas of all the triangular faces.
A cone is like a pyramid with a circular base: V = ⅓ × πr² × h follows the same rule.

example.q: A square pyramid has base side 6 m, height 4 m and slant height (of each triangular face) 5 m. Find its volume and total surface area.

learn.reallife: Glass pyramids above museums and paper lampshades use pyramid surface area for material and volume for the space inside.

revise.summary: A pyramid has a polygon base and triangular faces meeting at the apex. Volume = ⅓ × base area × height; surface area = base + all triangular faces.
focus: Find surface areas of square pyramids.
remember: Base 6, height 4, slant 5: V = 48 m³, TSA = 96 m².
Pyramid = ⅓ of a prism with the same base and height.
Number of triangular faces = number of base sides.

learn.hook: Archimedes was so proud of this that he wanted it carved on his tomb: a sphere inside a cylinder!
points: A sphere is the set of all points in space at the same distance r from a centre.
Surface area = 4πr². Archimedes showed this equals the curved surface area of the cylinder that just encloses the sphere (radius r, height 2r): 2πr × 2r = 4πr².
Volume = (4/3)πr³, which is exactly 2/3 of the enclosing cylinder's volume πr² × 2r = 2πr³.

Hands-on: wind a string tightly over half a ball (a hemisphere), then use the same length of string to fill circles of the ball's radius. A whole ball needs string to fill exactly 4 such circles, so its surface is 4πr².

example.q: A ball has radius 7 cm. Find its surface area and volume. (π = 22/7)

learn.reallife: Cricket balls, footballs and laddoos are close to spheres; makers use 4πr² for leather and (4/3)πr³ for filling.

games.title: Archimedes check

It is two-thirds.
The string on a ball fills 4 circles of the ball's radius.
That gives 4πr².
Every point on a sphere is the same distance from its centre.
That is the definition.
The enclosing cylinder of a sphere has height r.
Its height is 2r.

revise.summary: A sphere's surface 4πr² equals the curved surface of its enclosing cylinder, and its volume (4/3)πr³ is 2/3 of that cylinder's volume, as Archimedes found.
focus: Find surface area and volume of spheres.
remember: Sphere = ⅔ of the cylinder's volume.

topics.title: Maps, growing balls and hemisphere problems

learn.hook: On many world maps Greenland looks as big as Africa. In reality Africa is about 14 times bigger!
points: A cylindrical map projection wraps a cylinder around the globe and transfers the surface onto it. Near the equator it is fairly accurate, but near the poles the map gets badly distorted (on the common Mercator map, regions near the poles look much bigger than they really are).
If a sphere's radius is multiplied by k, its surface area is multiplied by k² and its volume by k³. A 10% larger radius gives 21% more area and 33.1% more volume.

Hemisphere problems: a dome's curved surface is 2πr² (for painting); a solid hemisphere's total surface is 3πr²; a hemispherical shell with outer radius R and inner radius r has volume (2/3)π(R³ − r³).

example.q: A hemispherical dome of radius 7 m is painted at ₹12 per m². Find the cost. (π = 22/7)

learn.reallife: Temple and mosque domes, gol gumbaz and planetarium roofs are hemispheres; painters estimate cost from 2πr².

games.title: Map and dome facts

The globe's surface is stretched most there to fit the cylinder.
On the Mercator map Greenland looks bigger than it really is compared to Africa.
Africa is about 14 times larger.
Painting a dome needs the area 3πr².
Only the curved part, 2πr², is painted.
A hemispherical shell's volume uses R³ − r³.
Outer minus inner hemisphere.
Doubling a ball's radius doubles its volume.
Volume becomes 8 times.

learn.hook: How many golgappas does India eat in a day? Nobody counts, but you can make a smart guess!
points: Everyday objects match solids: a gas cylinder (cylinder), a laddoo (sphere), a matchbox (cuboid), an ice-cream cone (cone plus hemisphere). Use the matching formula to estimate volumes.
Units: 1 litre = 1000 cm³, 1 m³ = 1000 litres, 1 m² = 10,000 cm².
Guesstimation: make clear, reasonable assumptions, round numbers, and combine them to get a sensible estimate (often just to the nearest power of 10).
Different assumptions give different answers: the number of tennis balls in a room depends on the room size and how tightly they pack. State your assumptions.
Projects: water you drink in a lifetime (≈ 2 L a day × 365 × 70 years ≈ 51,000 L), ink in a pen, volume of your house.

example.q: Estimate the litres of water a person drinks in 70 years at 2 L a day.

revise.summary: Everyday objects match solids, so their volumes can be estimated. Guesstimates state clear assumptions, round numbers and combine them; different assumptions can give different sensible answers.

Estimation is not random guessing.

topics.title: The Earth-string puzzle and cube formulas

learn.hook: Tie a string around the Earth's equator, then add just 1 metre. Could a cat crawl under it? Surprisingly, yes!
points: Earth-string puzzle: circumference C = 2πR. Adding 1 m makes C + 1 = 2π(R + gap), so gap = 1/(2π) ≈ 0.16 m, about 16 cm.
The gap does not depend on R at all: the same 16 cm for a football, the Earth or the Sun.
For a cube of edge a: V = a³ and S = 6a². Since a = V^(1/3), S = 6V^(2/3).
Example: V = 64 cm³ gives a = 4 and S = 6 × 16 = 96 cm². Doubling the volume does not double the surface; it multiplies it by 2^(2/3) ≈ 1.59.

example.q: A string is wrapped tightly around a football (radius 11 cm). It is lengthened by 1 m. How big is the gap now?
steps: About 16 cm, the same as for the Earth

learn.reallife: Puzzles like this show why we trust algebra over gut feeling.
